summary: This informational document, from the IRTF Coding for Efficient Network Communications Research Group, recommends terminology for network coding. It provides a set of terms to avoid ambiguity in future IRTF and IETF documents.

plainLanguage.summary: Everyone should call things by the same names. This is a word list for a topic about mixing data to send it better.

subtitle: Standard vocabulary for describing network coding techniques and concepts.

tldr.problem: Network coding research uses inconsistent terminology, leading to ambiguity in technical documents and making collaboration difficult across IETF and IRTF work.
tldr.mechanism: This document provides a comprehensive set of standard terms and definitions for network coding concepts, covering everything from basic packet and symbol definitions to advanced coding techniques like random linear coding and sliding-window codes.
tldr.outcome: Having shared terminology helps researchers and protocol designers communicate precisely about network coding approaches and facilitates the development of compatible specifications.

facts.label: Scope
facts.value: Packet erasure channels only (no bit-error channels)

today: RFC 8406 provides the standard terminology for network coding used in IETF specifications and IRTF research. It is still the reference for consistent vocabulary in this domain.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
This document is the product of the Coding for Efficient Network Communications Research Group (NWCRG). It summarizes recommended terminology for network coding, a technique where coding can be performed at the source, at intermediate forwarding nodes, or both. The goals include improving network throughput, efficiency, latency, and scalability, as well as providing resilience.

The document focuses on packet transmissions and losses in packet erasure channels (where packets are either dropped completely or received without error). It is in line with terminology from existing IETF working groups including RMT and FECFRAME.
sections.plainLanguage: Network coding lets you mix data in clever ways to send it more reliably. Different people were using different names for the same things, so this document says what everyone should call things.

sections.title: Core Concepts
sections.content:
Network coding divides data into basic units called symbols. A source symbol (or original payload) is a unit of data from the source. A repair symbol (or coded symbol) is created by encoding operations on source and repair symbols. These are sent in packets over the network.

Encoding takes source symbols as input and produces encoding symbols (source or repair). Recoding takes encoding symbols and produces new encoding symbols. Decoding takes encoding symbols and recovers the original source symbols. Systematic coding means the original source symbols are included unchanged in the output, alongside repair symbols.

End-to-End Coding is when coding happens only at the source and destination. Network Coding (the broader case) allows recoding at intermediate forwarding nodes.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of symbols as ingredients. A recipe combines ingredients (encoding), another chef mixes the result with other ingredients (recoding), and finally someone unmixes it to get back the original ingredients (decoding). Systematic means you keep some original ingredients in there unchanged.

sections.title: Coding Techniques
sections.content:
Linear Coding combines input symbols using coefficients in a finite field. Random Linear Coding (RLC) uses randomly chosen coefficients. Block Coding segments the input flow into blocks and encodes each block independently. Sliding Window Coding (or convolutional coding) generates repair symbols from a moving window of source symbols, allowing more flexibility than block coding.

Rateless Coding can generate unlimited repair symbols from a given set of source symbols (RLC is an example). Non-rateless Coding has a predefined maximum number of repair symbols.

The Code Rate is the ratio of source symbols to total symbols (source plus repair). A code rate of 0.5 means half repair symbols, half source symbols.
sections.plainLanguage: Linear coding mixes ingredients using math. Random linear coding uses random recipes. Block coding breaks the food into batches and cooks each batch separately. Sliding window coding is like a conveyor belt where you always have a moving window of ingredients to work with.

sections.title: Practical Implementation
sections.content:
An FEC Scheme is a complete specification that defines a particular code plus the protocol aspects needed to use it. This includes in-band signaling (information in packet headers) and out-of-band signaling (information in session descriptions).

The Encoding Symbol Identifier (ESI) uniquely identifies each source or repair symbol within a block or window. The FEC Payload ID identifies the contents of a packet with respect to the FEC scheme, typically containing the ESI plus information needed for decoding.

Key concepts for the receiver include the Decoding Window (the set of source symbols being decoded) and the Rank of the payload set (the number of linearly independent equations, also called degrees of freedom).
sections.plainLanguage: To use coding, you need to tell the receiver how to decode: what special numbers are in each packet (ESI), and what coding method you used. The receiver counts how many independent pieces of information it has received to know if it can decode.
